name: Anton and Permutation
description: Anton likes permutations, especially he likes to permute their elements. Note that a permutation of n elements is a sequence of numbers { a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n } , in which every number from 1 to n appears exactly once. One day Anton got a new permutation and started to play with it. He does the following operation q times: he takes two elements of the permutation and swaps these elements. After each operation he asks his friend Vanya, how many inversions there are in the new permutation. The number of inversions in a permutation is the number of distinct pairs ( i , j ) such that 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n and a i > a j . Vanya is tired of answering Anton's silly questions. So he asked you to write a program that would answer these questions instead of him. Initially Anton's permutation was {1, 2, ..., n } , that is a i = i for all i such that 1 ≤ i ≤ n .
input_specification: The first line of the input contains two integers n and q (1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000, 1 ≤ q ≤ 50 000) — the length of the permutation and the number of operations that Anton does. Each of the following q lines of the input contains two integers l i and r i (1 ≤ l i , r i ≤ n ) — the indices of elements that Anton swaps during the i -th operation. Note that indices of elements that Anton swaps during the i -th operation can coincide. Elements in the permutation are numbered starting with one.
output_specification: Output q lines. The i -th line of the output is the number of inversions in the Anton's permutation after the i -th operation.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 785E — Anton and Permutation [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
